notes.meaning: A severe famine struck the land of Israel for three years in a row, leading King David to pray and seek the Lord. God revealed that the dry years were a punishment for King Saul, who had cruelly put Gibeonites to death. Even though years had passed, God had not forgotten the broken promise, because time does not erase the guilt of sin. Unconfessed sin can bring hardship on an entire nation until it is made right.

David called the Gibeonites together to talk with them about what Saul had done. The Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a surviving group of Amorites whom Israel had sworn to protect centuries earlier in the days of Joshua. Saul had broken that sacred national vow by trying to wipe them out, claiming he was acting out of religious zeal. Good intentions or national pride never make up for breaking a solemn promise made before God.

David asked the Gibeonites what he could do to make amends and restore peace between them and Israel. To make amends (or atonement) means to remove the guilt of sin so that God's favor can return. David wanted the Gibeonites to pray for a blessing on the Lord's people instead of carrying unhealed hurt. Restoring broken relationships is essential for receiving God's blessing.

The Gibeonites answered that they did not want money from Saul's estate, nor did they have the right to execute ordinary Israelites. Under God's law, money could never pay for the loss of innocent human life. David then told them he would grant whatever just solution they asked for.

The Gibeonites asked that seven male descendants of Saul be handed over to them so they could execute them at Saul's hometown of Gibeah. In the Bible, the number seven represents completeness, showing that full public justice would be done. David agreed to their request, knowing that Saul's royal family had to answer for the bloodguilt brought on the country. God's justice requires that wrongdoing be addressed openly and completely.

David protected Jonathan's son Mephibosheth from being handed over to the Gibeonites. Years earlier, David and Jonathan had sworn a lifelong covenant of friendship and loyalty to each other before God. While David was righting the wrong of Saul's broken vow, he made sure not to break his own vow to Jonathan. God honors those who keep their promises even when times are difficult.

David chose two sons born to Saul through his concubine Rizpah, along with five grandsons born to Saul's daughter Merab. These seven men represented Saul's royal household to pay the penalty for the slaughter of the Gibeonites. Many commentators suggest these relatives may have taken an active part in carrying out Saul's cruel attacks. Sin often brings sorrow and consequences that affect an entire family line.

The Gibeonites executed the seven men on a hill before the Lord right as the spring barley harvest began. The public execution showed everyone that the curse Saul had brought on the nation was finally being removed. Dying exposed on a hill bore the mark of divine judgment so the land could be cleansed. Removing the curse of sin opens the way for God's blessings to return.

Rizpah, the mother of two of the dead men, spread rough sackcloth on a rock to make a simple shelter. She kept watch day and night to keep birds and wild animals from tearing the bodies until rain finally poured down from heaven. Her fierce devotion showed a mother's deep love and grief even in the middle of a terrible national tragedy.

King David was told about Rizpah's faithful, lonely vigil over the bodies of her sons. Hearing about her extraordinary grief and loyalty moved David with deep compassion. Instead of being angry, David was inspired by her love to show honor to the whole house of Saul.

David went and gathered the bones of King Saul and his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead. Brave men from that city had secretly rescued the bodies long before, after the Philistines had hung them on the wall of Beth-shan. David wanted to give Israel's first king and his dear friend a proper and honorable burial.

David brought back the remains of Saul and Jonathan and also gathered the bones of the seven men who had been executed. He made sure that none of Saul's descendants were left out in the open or neglected in death. This kind act proved that David acted out of obedience to God rather than personal hatred against Saul's family.

Saul and Jonathan were buried together in the tomb of Saul's father Kish in the land of Benjamin. Once everything David commanded had been carried out and justice was done, God answered the prayers of the people and healed the land. When we humble ourselves and turn away from past wrongdoing, God is quick to show mercy and bring relief.

War broke out once more between the Philistines and Israel, and David led his soldiers out to fight. During the heavy combat, the aging king grew faint and exhausted. Even the greatest leaders and fighters eventually reach the physical limits of old age.

A giant Philistine warrior named Ishbi-benob saw that David was tired and decided to kill him. This warrior carried a heavy bronze spear point weighing about eight pounds and was armed with fresh weapons. The enemies of God often try to strike believers when they are at their weakest.

Abishai rushed in to rescue David and struck down the Philistine giant. After this close call, David's men made him promise never to go into battle again, calling him the lamp of Israel. David's life was like a light guiding the whole nation, and God used loyal friends to protect him when his own strength ran out.

Later on, another battle against the Philistines took place at Gob. In this clash, an Israelite warrior named Sibbecai killed Saph, another giant of the ancient Rephaim line. God gave Israel victory over huge enemies even when David was no longer swinging a sword on the battlefield.

During another fight at Gob, Elhanan from Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath the Philistine. This enemy carried a massive spear with a heavy shaft like a weaver's beam, just like Goliath had carried years before. God raised up other courageous soldiers to finish wiping out the terrifying enemies who threatened His people.

Another battle took place at Gath against a giant who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. He was also born from the ancient race of giants and relied on his unusual size to frighten Israel. Physical power and unusual size are never enough to overcome God's strength.

When this giant dared to taunt and mock the army of Israel, Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimei, killed him. Just as David had faced Goliath's insults years earlier, David's nephew stepped forward with faith to silence the enemy. God gives His people boldness to stand firm against those who mock Him.

These four giant warriors from Gath were all defeated by David and the brave men who served him. David began his public life by killing one giant, and by the end of his life his soldiers had learned how to conquer giants too. A faithful leader leaves behind a legacy of people who know how to win battles in God's strength.
